title: Doodhi Halwa: How to Make the Classic Bottle Gourd Dessert Without Khoya
excerpt: This simplified Punjabi recipe turns a humble lauki into a rich, cardamom-scented halwa in under 45 minutes — no specialty ingredients required.
body:
• Doodhi halwa (lauki ka halwa) is a beloved North Indian dessert made from grated bottle gourd, milk, sugar, ghee, and cardamom — with no khoya required in this simplified version.
  • The dish takes about 40-45 minutes to prepare and costs as little as ₹20-30 for the main ingredient, making it one of the most affordable traditional Indian sweets.
  • Bottle gourd is rich in fiber and water content, making doodhi halwa a lighter alternative to heavier milk-based mithai like gulab jamun or barfi.
  • The recipe works best when the lauki is fresh, firm, and free of bitterness — always taste a raw slice before cooking.

The Humble Gourd That Became a Royal Dessert

In the sprawling repertoire of Indian sweets, doodhi halwa occupies a quiet but firm position. Known variously as lauki ka halwa, dudhi ka halwa, or bottle gourd halwa, this Punjabi classic transforms one of India's cheapest vegetables into a rich, cardamom-scented dessert that holds its own alongside the most elaborate mithai.

The beauty of doodhi halwa lies in its simplicity. A single bottle gourd — available at most Indian grocery stores for under a dollar — yields enough halwa for a family of four. Unlike many Indian sweets that demand khoya (reduced milk solids) or hours of stirring, this version relies on the gourd's own moisture and a slow cook with milk to create that characteristic silky texture.

What You Need

The ingredient list is short: one large bottle gourd (doodhi or lauki), peeled and thickly grated; two cups of full-fat milk; half a cup of sugar (adjust to taste); three to four tablespoons of ghee; half a teaspoon of cardamom powder; and a handful of chopped cashews, almonds, and chironji nuts for garnish. Optional additions include saffron strands for color and rose petals for presentation.

A quick note on the bottle gourd: always taste a raw slice before committing to the recipe. Bitter lauki contains compounds called cucurbitacins that can cause stomach distress. If it tastes bitter, discard it entirely.

The Method

Heat two tablespoons of ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan or kadhai over medium flame. Add the grated bottle gourd and sauté for four to five minutes until it softens and the raw smell dissipates. The moisture from the gourd will release during this stage — let it cook off rather than draining it, as it carries flavor.

Meanwhile, bring the milk to a boil separately. A pinch of baking soda added to the boiling milk helps it reduce faster and gives the halwa a slightly richer color. Pour the hot milk into the sautéed gourd and stir well. Cook on medium flame for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring frequently to prevent sticking, until the milk is almost fully absorbed.

Add sugar once the mixture has thickened. The sugar will release additional moisture, so continue cooking for another five to eight minutes until the halwa pulls away from the sides of the pan. Finish with cardamom powder and the remaining ghee. The halwa should be glossy, thick, and fragrant.

"Doodhi halwa tops the chart of all-time favourite Indian mithai. Whether you have it cold, right out of the fridge, or warm it up and have it plain or with a topping of ice-cream, it is sure to charm you with its rich texture and enticing flavour."

— Tarla Dalal, Indian culinary authority

The Garnish Makes It

In a separate small pan, heat a teaspoon of ghee and fry cashews, almonds, and chironji until golden. Scatter these over the halwa along with saffron strands if using. For a festive touch, add silver vark (edible silver leaf) and fresh rose petals.

Doodhi halwa works beautifully both warm and chilled. Served warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream, it becomes an Indo-fusion dessert. Refrigerated overnight, it firms up enough to cut into squares — perfect for a mithai box or a potluck contribution.

Why Diaspora Cooks Love It

For Indians abroad, doodhi halwa checks several boxes. Bottle gourd is increasingly available at Indian grocery stores and mainstream supermarkets in the US, UK, and Canada. The recipe requires no specialty equipment — just a heavy pan and a grater. And it produces results that look and taste far more impressive than the effort involved.

The dessert also adapts well to dietary preferences. Substituting coconut oil for ghee and coconut milk for dairy milk creates a vegan version that retains much of the original's character. Reducing sugar and adding dates or jaggery offers a less refined alternative that many health-conscious diaspora families prefer.

Storage and Serving

Doodhi halwa keeps well in the refrigerator for three to four days and freezes for up to a month. Reheat with a splash of milk to restore its creamy consistency. The prep-to-plate time of roughly 40 minutes makes it viable even for weeknight desserts — a rarity in traditional Indian sweet-making, where many recipes demand an afternoon of effort.
